# On soliton clusters and collision blow up for the $L^{2}$ -critical Hartree equation

**Authors:** Tobias Schmid Address: University of Vienna, Faculty of Mathematics, Oskar-Morgenstern-Platz 1, 1090 Vienna Email address: tobias.schmid@univie.ac.at and Yutong Wu Address: Department of Mathematics, Yale University, New Haven, CT 06511 Email address: yutong.wu.yw894@yale.edu

## Abstract

We consider the $L^{2}$ -critical nonlinear Hartree equation in $\R^{1+4}$ and multisoliton solutions for which the trajectories are approximated to leading order by an $m$ -body law. We obtain soliton clusters asymptotically following hyperbolic-parabolic trajectories of the corresponding $m$ -body problem. By pseudo-conformal invariance, we then conclude finite-time collision blow-up with any number of clusters, each consisting of an arbitrary number of solitons, colliding simultaneously at distinct prescribed points.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Setting of the problem

We consider the $L^{2}$ -critical nonlinear Hartree equation, i.e. we study the following cubic Schrödinger equation

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\;\;i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u-\phi_{|u|^{2}}u=0,\;\;(t,x)\in[0,T)\times\R^{4}&\\[2.0pt]
\;\;u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\;\;x\in\R^{4},&\end{cases} $$

where we set $\phi_{|u|^{2}}$ to be the convolution of $|u|^{2}$ with the inverse square potential, i.e.

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{|u|^{2}}=-\frac{1}{|x|^{2}}\ast|u|^{2},\;\;x\in\R^{4}, $$

and therefore $\Delta\Phi=|u|^{2}$ for $\Phi=\kappa\phi_{|u|^{2}}$ with a constant $\kappa=\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}$ . Hence the nonlinearity in (1.1) models a gravitational coupling which introduces long-range effects and typically appears for instance related to the mean field dynamics of Bose gases, cf. [5] and Boson stars, see [3], [14]. It is well known, see [1, 6], that (1.1) is locally wellposed in $H^{1}(\R^{4})$ . In particular (1.1) is a Hamiltonian equation for which $H^{1}$ -solutions conserve energy, mass and momentum

$$ \displaystyle\text{\emph{Hamiltonian\;energy}}:\;\;\hskip 0.0pt\mathcal{E}(u(t))=\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla u(t)|^{2}\;\mathrm{d}x-\frac{\kappa}{4}\int|\nabla\phi_{|u(t)|^{2}}|^{2}\;\mathrm{d}x=\mathcal{E}(u_{0}), \displaystyle\text{\emph{$L^{2}$-norm (mass)}}:\;\;\hskip 0.0pt\int|u(t)|^{2}\;\mathrm{d}x=\int|u_{0}|^{2}\;\mathrm{d}x, L^{2} \displaystyle\text{\emph{Momentum}}:\;\;\hskip 0.0pt\text{Im}\bigg(\int\nabla u(t)\cdot\overline{u(t)}\;\mathrm{d}x\bigg)=\text{Im}\bigg(\int\nabla u_{0}\cdot\overline{u_{0}}\;\mathrm{d}x\bigg). $$

The equation (1.1) has the following symmetries

$$ \displaystyle u(t,x)\mapsto\lambda^{2}u(\lambda^{2}t+t_{0},\lambda x-\alpha-\beta t)e^{i(\frac{1}{2}\beta\cdot x-\frac{1}{4}|\beta|^{2}t+\gamma)}, $$

where $\lambda\in\R_{+},t_{0}\in\R,\alpha,\beta\in\R^{4},\gamma\in\R$ , meaning if $u(t,x)$ is a solution of (1.1), then $u_{\lambda,t_{0},\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(t,x)$ defined via (1.6) is a solution of (1.1). Further if $u\in C^{0}([0,T),H^{1}(\R^{4}))$ is a solution of (1.1) and blows up at $t=T$ , then

$$ \limsup_{t\to T^{-}}\|\nabla u\|_{L_{x}^{2}}^{2}=\infty. $$

In fact, blow-up with $\mathcal{E}(u_{0})<0$ follows from the virial law

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\int|x|^{2}|u(t,x)|^{2}\;\mathrm{d}x=16\mathcal{E}(u_{0}), $$

hence all solutions in $H^{1}\cap L^{2}(|x|^{2}\mathrm{d}x)$ blow up in finite time if $\mathcal{E}(u_{0})<0$ . Moreover, equation (1.1) has soliton solutions $u_{\omega}(t,x)=e^{i\omega^{2}t}Q_{\omega}(x)$ , where $Q_{\omega}=\omega^{2}Q_{1}(\omega\cdot)$ and $Q:=Q_{1}$ is the unique radial positive $H^{1}$ -solution of

$$ \displaystyle\Delta Q-\phi_{|Q|^{2}}Q=Q,\;\;x\in\R^{4}. $$

Such $Q$ is called the ground state. The existence follows from the adaption of [24] and for uniqueness we refer to [13] (in $d=3$ ), as well as [11, Section 4] in $d=4$ . By using Gagliardo-Nirenberg interpolation and Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev’s inequality,

$$ \mathcal{E}(u)\geq\|\nabla u\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\bigg(1-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}_{x}}}{\|u\|_{L^{2}_{x}}}\bigg),\;\;u\in H^{1}(\R^{4}), $$

and hence the solutions of (1.1) are global if $u_{0}\in H^{1}(\R^{4})$ with $\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{x}}<\|Q\|_{L^{2}_{x}}$ . This is sharp due to the pseudo-conformal symmetry, i.e. if $u(t,x)$ solves (1.1), then so does

$$ \displaystyle u(t,x)\mapsto\frac{1}{t^{2}}\overline{u}(\frac{1}{t},\frac{x}{t})e^{i\frac{|x|^{2}}{4t}}. $$

In particular, applying the symmetry to $e^{it}Q(x)$ we obtain a minimal mass blow-up solution

$$ S(t,x)=\frac{1}{t^{2}}Q(\frac{x}{t})e^{i(-\frac{1}{t}+\frac{|x|^{2}}{4t})}, $$

which satisfies $\|S(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}=\|Q\|_{L^{2}_{x}}$ and $\|\nabla S(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\sim|t|^{-1},\;t\to 0^{-}$ . For radial data, Krieger-Lenzmann-Raphaël [11] proved the finite-codimension stability of $S(t)$ . Besides the pseudo-conformal rate, formal and numerical calculations in [27] reveal further log-log blow-up mechanisms as for the $L^{2}$ -critical (local) NLS.

Literature. Recently, in [7], the authors have constructed multisoliton solutions of (1.1) with modulation trajectories following non-trapped solutions (parabolic and hyperbolic trajectories) of an $m$ -body problem derived from the Newton potential $|x|^{-2}$ . Via the pseudo-conformal invariance, this leads to blow-up at any number of distinct points of multiplicity one, and collision blow-up at a single point of any multiplicity (see [7, Section 1.3]). The method of proof applied in [7] was pioneered for the 3D Hartree-NLS by Krieger-Martel-Raphaël [12] for two-soliton solutions along asymptotically hyperbolic/parabolic orbits. Subsequently, this approach was extended by the second author [25] to 3D multisoliton solutions following hyperbolic, parabolic and hyperbolic-parabolic motion. In comparison to (1.1), the $L^{2}$ -critical NLS

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u=-|u|^{\frac{4}{d}}u\;\;\text{in}\;\;\R^{1+d} $$

is well studied concerning $H^{1}$ -blow-up and solitary dynamics, see the overview in [7, Section 1] and [17, Section 1] for instance. Multisoliton solutions for (1.9) have been proved to exist in [18], [17], [22], [4] and generally provide a description of large data solutions, see in particular [16], [10], [23], [2], [21] for the construction and stability results in NLS equations. More relevant for our present work is the strong interaction regime, see [12], [25], [17], [20] for which we also refer to strongly interacting kinks of $(1+1)$ -scalar fields [9], [8]. In particular in the latter work a (very different) 1-dimensional $m$ -body approximation is used to derive the trajectories to leading order. In this article, we extend the multisoliton result [7, Section 1.3] and obtain solutions of (1.1) with modulation trajectories asymptotic to hyperbolic-parabolic orbits of a suitable $m$ -body law (1.10) (see Theorem 1.2). Further, by applying the pseudo-conformal transformation, we obtain finite-time collision blow-up at the pseudo-conformal rate with multiple soliton trajectories colliding simultaneously at multiple distinct prescribed points (see Corollary 1.4).

The $m$ -body law. Let $m\in\Z_{\geq 2}$ and $\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{m})\in\R^{4m}$ be the configuration of $m$ bodies with center $\alpha_{j}\in\R^{4}$ . We consider (c.f. [7, Section 1.2]) the following $m$ -body law

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\;\;\dot{\alpha}_{j}(t)=2\beta_{j}(t),\;\;1\leq j\leq m,\;&\\[5.0pt]
\;\;\displaystyle\dot{\beta}_{j}(t)=-\|Q\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}}{|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|^{4}}.&\end{cases} $$

The system (1.10) has a first integral $H=K-U$ , where

$$ \displaystyle K(\beta)=2\sum_{j=1}^{m}|\beta_{j}(t)|^{2},\;\;U(\alpha)=\|Q\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\sum_{j<k}\frac{1}{|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|^{2}}, $$

are the kinetic- and potential energy respectively. Following the idea in [12, 25] and [7], the trajectories of solutions $(\alpha(t),\beta(t))$ to (1.10) will provide leading asymptotics of the modulation variables through applying (1.6) to the ground state $Q$ . The center of mass $M(t):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{j}(t)\displaystyle$ evolves by free Galilean motion. Let us recall (see [7]) the set of central configurations and the non-collision set

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{X}:=\big\{x=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m})\in\R^{4m}\;|\;{\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}=0}\big\},\;\;\mathcal{Y}:=\mathcal{X}\setminus\Delta, \displaystyle\Delta:=\big\{x=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m})\in\mathcal{X}\;|\;\exists\;j\neq k:x_{j}=x_{k}\big\}. $$

Further we set $\alpha_{jk}=\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}$ and the minimal distance $a:=\min_{j<k}|\alpha_{jk}|$ . For global solutions $\alpha(t)$ to (1.10) we have in particular (c.f. the argument in [15])

$$ \max_{j<k}|\alpha_{jk}(t)|=O(t)\;\text{as}\;t\to+\infty,\;\;\liminf_{t\to+\infty}a(t)>0. $$

Moreover, for some $v\in\mathcal{X}$ (the limit velocity) we have $\alpha(t)=vt+O(t^{\frac{1}{2}})$ as $t\to+\infty$ . Expansive orbits. If $a(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ , we say $\alpha(t)$ is an expansive orbit. Let us recall from [7, Section 1.2] the following definition for expansive solutions.

- (1) We say $(\alpha(t),\beta(t))$ is hyperbolic, if $v\in\mathcal{Y}$ , i.e., $|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\sim t$ as $t\to+\infty$ for all $j\neq k$ .

- (2) We say $(\alpha(t),\beta(t))$ is parabolic, if $v=0$ and $|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\sim t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ as $t\to+\infty$ for all $j\neq k$ .

- (3) We say $(\alpha(t),\beta(t))$ is hyperbolic-parabolic, if $v\in\Delta\setminus\{0\}$ and $|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\sim t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ as $t\to+\infty$ for all $j\neq k$ such that $v_{j}=v_{k}$ .

Clusters. In the hyperbolic-parabolic case (3), we define a cluster partition via the equivalence relation $j\sim k$ if and only if $v_{j}=v_{k}$ , i.e., $|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{k}(t)|\sim t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ . Each equivalence class is called a cluster. Now assuming there are $l$ clusters $\{K_{i}\}_{i=1}^{l}$ , then we may define the cluster energy

$$ U_{K_{i}}(\alpha)=\|Q\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j<k\\
j,k\in K_{i}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|^{2}},\quad\tilde{U}(\alpha)=\sum_{i=1}^{l}U_{K_{i}}(\alpha), $$

and thus $U(\alpha)=\tilde{U}(\alpha)+O(t^{-2})$ as $t\to+\infty$ . The following proposition guaranties the existence of hyperbolic-parabolic solutions of (1.10) for any prescribed limiting velocities.

#### Proposition 1.1.

Let $v\in\Delta\setminus\{0\}$ and $\{K_{i}\}$ be the clusters. For each $i$ , assume $(\alpha_{j}^{0},\beta_{j}^{0})$ , $j\in K_{i}$ is a parabolic solution to the $|K_{i}|$ -body problem. Then there exists a hyperbolic-parabolic solution $(\alpha,\beta)$ to the $m$ -body problem (1.10) with

$$ \alpha_{j}(t)=v_{j}t+\alpha_{j}^{0}(t)+o(t^{-1+})\;\;\text{as}\;\;t\to+\infty. $$

#### Sketch of the proof.

Let $\tilde{\alpha}_{j}(t)=v_{j}t+\alpha_{j}^{0}(t)$ . Then

$$ \ddot{\tilde{\alpha}}=\nabla\tilde{U}(\tilde{\alpha})=\nabla U(\tilde{\alpha})+O(t^{-3}). $$

For $x=\alpha-\tilde{\alpha}$ , by the Taylor formula, we obtain

$$ \ddot{x}=\nabla U(\alpha)-\nabla U(\tilde{\alpha})+O(t^{-3})=\nabla^{2}U(\tilde{\alpha})x+O(t^{-3}) $$

with the bootstrap assumption $x(t)=o(t^{-1+})$ . Further, there exists $A\in\R^{4m\times 4m}$ and $\epsilon>0$ such that $\nabla^{2}U(\tilde{\alpha})=t^{-2}A+O(t^{-2-\epsilon})$ . Thus we have

$$ \ddot{x}=\frac{Ax}{t^{2}}+O(t^{-3}), $$

for which we may use the argument in [7, Lemma 4.4] to find $x$ . ∎

We refer to [26, Theorem 3] for a more general result with detailed proof.

### 1.2. Statement of the results

Here we state our main results in this article, which is an extension of the construction in [7, Section 1.3] to the case of hyperbolic-parabolic trajectories.

#### Theorem 1.2.

Let $(\alpha^{\infty},\beta^{\infty})$ be a hyperbolic-parabolic solution to (1.10) and $\lambda_{j}^{\infty}>0$ such that for $j\neq k$ , $\lambda_{j}^{\infty}=\lambda_{k}^{\infty}$ whenever $|\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)-\alpha_{k}^{\infty}(t)|\sim t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ as $t\to+\infty$ . Then there exist a solution $u\in C^{0}([0,+\infty),H^{1}(\R^{4}))$ to (1.1) and $\gamma^{\infty}(t)$ with

$$ \bigg\|u(t,\cdot)-\sum_{j=1}^{m}Q_{\lambda_{j}^{\infty}}\big(\cdot-\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)\big)e^{i\gamma_{j}^{\infty}(t)+i\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)\cdot x}\bigg\|_{H^{1}}=o(t^{-\frac{1}{2}+})\quad\text{as }t\to+\infty. $$

#### Remark 1.3.

Let $K_{1},\cdots,K_{l}$ be the clusters for $(\alpha^{\infty},\beta^{\infty})$ . Then for any $1\leq i\leq l$ , we consider

$$ \sum_{j\in K_{i}}Q_{\lambda_{j}^{\infty}}\big(\cdot-\alpha_{j}^{\infty}(t)\big)e^{i\gamma_{j}^{\infty}(t)+i\beta_{j}^{\infty}(t)\cdot x} $$

to be a soliton cluster. For each soliton cluster, there exists a Galilean transform such that the solitons within the cluster have vanishing velocities.

Recall $\Delta=\big\{x=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m})\in\R^{4m}\;|\;\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{j}=0\;\;\text{and}\;\;\exists\;j\neq k:x_{j}=x_{k}\big\}$ is the collision set, and $\Delta\setminus\{0\}$ represents the set of non-parabolic collision configurations.

#### Corollary 1.4 (Finite-time collision blow-up at multiple points with multiplicity).

Let $m\in\Z_{\geq 2}$ and $v\in\Delta\setminus\{0\}$ . Then (1.1) has a solution $u\in C^{0}((-\infty,0),H^{1}(\R^{4}))$ that blows up at $t=0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\sim|t|^{-1}\;\;\;\text{and}\;\;\;|u(t)|^{2}\rightharpoonup\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|Q\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}\delta_{v_{j}}\;\;\text{as}\;\;t\to 0^{-}. $$

Moreover, for any $\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{m}>0$ satisfying $\lambda_{j}=\lambda_{k}$ whenever $v_{j}=v_{k}$ , and any hyperbolic-parabolic solution $(\tilde{\alpha}(t),\tilde{\beta}(t))$ of the $m$ -body problem (1.10) satisfying

$$ \lim_{t\to+\infty}t^{-1}\tilde{\alpha}_{j}(t)=v_{j},\quad\forall j=1,2\cdots m, $$

there is a blow-up solution $u$ as above and $\gamma_{j}\in C^{0}(-\infty,0)$ , $\alpha_{j}(t)=|t|\tilde{\alpha}_{j}(|t|^{-1})$ , $\beta_{j}(t)=-|t|^{-1}\tilde{\beta}_{j}(|t|^{-1})$ , such that when writing

$$ u(t,x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{1}{t^{2}}Q_{\lambda_{j}}\Big(\frac{x-\alpha_{j}(t)}{t}\Big)e^{i(\gamma_{j}(t)+\beta_{j}(t)\cdot x+\frac{|x|^{2}}{4t})}+\varepsilon(t,x), $$

we have $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0^{-}}\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{L^{2}\cap L^{\frac{8}{3}^{-}}}=0$ .

The proof of Corollary 1.4 follows from Theorem 1.2 and the application of the pseudo-conformal transformation.

#### Remark 1.5.

The assumption $\sum_{j}x_{j}=0$ in the definition of $\Delta$ is without loss of generality by Galilean invariance of both (1.10) and (1.1).

#### Remark 1.6.

Examples of hyperbolic-parabolic $m$ -body trajectories are obtained from Proposition 1.1 together with [7, Proposition 1.5]. To be precise, for the hyperbolic-parabolic orbits $(\tilde{\alpha},\tilde{\beta})$ we constructed, there exists $b_{j}\in\R^{4}$ such that

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{j}(t)=v_{j}t+b_{j}t^{\frac{1}{2}}+o(t^{-1+}),\;\;\tilde{\beta}_{j}(t)=\frac{v_{j}}{2}+o(t^{-\frac{1}{2}+})\;\;\;\text{as}\;\;t\to+\infty,\;\;\forall\;1\leq j\leq m. $$

Thus, we observe for $(\alpha,\beta)$ in Corollary 1.4

$$ \alpha_{j}(t)=v_{j}+b_{j}|t|^{\frac{1}{2}}+O(|t|),\;\;\beta_{j}(t)=-\frac{v_{j}}{2|t|}+O(|t|^{-\frac{1}{2}})\;\;\text{as}\;\;\;t\to 0^{-},\;\;\forall\;1\leq j\leq m. $$

#### Remark 1.7.

(i) The solutions in Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.4 are strongly interacting in the sense of [17], i.e. the trajectories of the solitons are perturbed to leading order by the presence of the other solitons. An intricate question for finite-time blow-up of the $L^{2}$ -critical NLS is whether concentration scenarios

$$ \displaystyle|u(t)|^{2}\rightharpoonup\sum_{i=1}^{l}m_{i}\delta_{x_{i}}+|u^{*}|^{2}\;\;\text{as}\;\;t\to T^{-}, $$

appear for large masses (c.f. [19] in the weakly interacting regime) and which rates are possible. Here $m_{i}>0$ , $x_{1},\cdots,x_{l}$ are distinct and $u^{*}\in L^{2}$ . Corollary 1.4 shows that for (1.1), the asymptotics (1.21) with $u^{*}=0$ , $l\in\Z_{\geq 2}$ and $m_{i}=\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}k_{i}$ , $k_{i}\in\Z_{+}$ can be realized at the pseudo-conformal rate via strong interactions. (ii) To the authors’ knowledge, collision blow-up for the mass-critical NLS (1.9) is only known by the remarkable result in [17], where the blow-up is at a single point above the pseudo-conformal rate.

Outline. The article follows the strategy proposed in [12], [25] and [7]. In Section 2, we quote the non-degeneracy and the (finite co-dimension) coercivity properties of the linearized operators from [7]. In Section 3, we give details for the adapted construction of approximate solutions used in [25], [7] (see Remark 3.2), which ensures a small interaction error. This is followed by an analysis in Section 4 for the choice of the modulation parameters to satisfy the modulation ODE (4.1). In Section 5, we reduce the proof to a bootstrap argument by choosing a modulation path with suitable orthogonality conditions. In the last Section 6, we then control the modulation part of the bootstrap estimate by the analysis in Section 3 and Section 4, and lastly use coercivity and the orthogonality conditions to control the error in the energy space via the bootstrap estimate.

## 2. The ground state linearized operators

We linearize (1.1) at the ground state $Q$ via writing $u(t)=e^{it}(Q+\varepsilon(t))$ and separating $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{1}+i\varepsilon_{2}$ . This shows the leading operator has the form

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}0&-L_{-}\\
L_{+}&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\Delta-1\\
-\Delta+1&0\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0&-\phi_{Q^{2}}\\
\phi_{Q^{2}}+2Q\phi_{(\cdot\;Q)}&0\end{pmatrix} $$

when acting on $\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon_{1}\\ \varepsilon_{2}\end{pmatrix}$ and hence we identify

$$ \displaystyle L_{+}=-\Delta+1+\phi_{Q^{2}}+2Q\phi_{(\cdot\;Q)},\;\;L_{-}=-\Delta+1+\phi_{Q^{2}}. $$

In particular $L_{\pm}$ are posed on $L^{2}(\R^{4})$ with domain $D=H^{2}(\R^{4})\subset L^{2}(\R^{4})$ and we recall

$$ \phi_{Q^{2}}=-|x|^{-2}\ast Q^{2},\;\;\phi_{(\cdot\;Q)}=-|x|^{-2}\ast(\;\cdot\;Q),\;\; $$

thus $L_{+}$ is a non-local operator.

Let us now recall important non-degeneracy and inversion properties of $L_{\pm}$ proved in [7, Section 2], see also [11], [14]. We start with the generalized root space.

#### Lemma 2.1 ([7]).

a

- (i) $L_{\pm}$ are self-adjoint, $\emph{spec}_{\emph{c}}(L_{\pm})=[1,+\infty)$ , $0\in\emph{spec}(L_{\pm})$ and $L_{-}\geq 0$ .

- (ii) The following are elements of the generalized root space of the operator (2.1) $\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}0\\ Q\end{pmatrix},\;\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda Q\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\;\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{x_{j}}Q\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\;\begin{pmatrix}0\\ |x|^{2}Q\end{pmatrix},\;\begin{pmatrix}\rho(x)\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\;\begin{pmatrix}0\\ x_{j}Q\end{pmatrix},\;\;j=1,2,3,4,$ where $\Lambda=2+x\cdot\nabla$ and (2.3) $\displaystyle L_{-}Q=L_{+}(\partial_{x_{j}}Q)=0,\;L_{+}(\Lambda Q)=-2Q,\;L_{-}(|x|^{2}Q)=-4\Lambda Q,$ (2.4) $\displaystyle L_{-}(x_{j}Q)=-2\partial_{x_{j}}Q,\;L_{+}\rho=-|x|^{2}Q.$

- (iii) We have $\displaystyle(Q,\rho)=\frac{1}{2}(\Lambda Q,|x|^{2}Q)=-\frac{1}{2}\|xQ\|_{L^{2}}^{2},\;(Q,\Lambda Q)=0,$ $\displaystyle(xQ,\nabla Q)=-2\|Q\|^{2}_{L^{2}}.$

The following two Propositions will be essential in the next Section 3 and Section 5.

#### Proposition 2.2 ([7]).

- (1) We have non-degeneracy of the kernel of $L_{\pm}$ , i.e. if $L_{+}u=0$ , then $u=a\cdot\nabla Q$ for some $a\in\R^{4}$ . Likewise if $L_{-}u=0$ , then $u=bQ$ for some $b\in\R$ .

- (2) For all real-valued functions $v\in H^{1}$ we have the coercivity (2.5) $\displaystyle(L_{+}v,v)$ $\displaystyle\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2}-C(v,Q)^{2}-C(v,xQ)^{2}-C(v,|x|^{2}Q)^{2},$ $\displaystyle(L_{-}v,v)$ $\displaystyle\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2}-C(v,\rho)^{2},$ where $c,C>0$ are positive constants (independent of $v$ ).

#### Proposition 2.3 ([7]).

Let $f$ be a real-valued admissible function of degree $n\in\N$ . Then we have the following

- (1) If $\langle f,\nabla Q\rangle=0$ , there exists a real-valued admissible solution to $L_{+}u=f$ of degree $n$ .

- (2) If $\langle f,Q\rangle=0$ , there exists a real-valued admissible solution to $L_{-}u=f$ of degree $n$ . Further if $f$ is radial, then $u$ can be chosen radial.

## 3. Construction of approximate solutions

We let $\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{m})$ and similarly for $(\beta$ , $\lambda$ , $\mu$ , $\delta$ , $\gamma$ ), which are (possibly) time dependent parameters . We also denote

$$ \begin{split}&P=(\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu,\delta),\quad g=(P,\gamma),\quad g_{j}=(P_{j},\gamma_{j})=(\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},\lambda_{j},\mu_{j},\delta_{j},\gamma_{j}),\\[3.0pt]
&\alpha_{jk}=\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k},\quad\beta_{jk}=\beta_{j}-\beta_{k},\quad a=\min_{j\neq k}|\alpha_{jk}|.\end{split} $$

For a function $v:\R\times\R^{4}\to\C$ we then modulate via the path $g_{j}=(P_{j},\gamma_{j})$

$$ g_{j}v(t,x):=\lambda_{j}^{2}v\big(t,\lambda_{j}(x-\alpha_{j})\big)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x+i\mu_{j}|x|^{2}}. $$

In particular, we set $u_{j}(t,x)=g_{j}v_{j}(t,x)$ and assume the $v_{j}$ ’s are functions of $\alpha_{j}$ , $\beta_{j}$ , $\lambda_{j}$ , $\gamma_{j}$ , $\mu_{j}$ and the spatial variable. If we set

$$ u(t,x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_{j}(t,x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}v_{j}(t,x) $$

then it is, after some calculations, straightforward to observe the expression

$$ i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u-\phi_{|u|^{2}}u=\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_{j}(t,y_{j})e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x+i\mu_{j}|x|^{2}}-\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{Re(u_{k}\overline{u_{j}})}u, $$

where $y_{j}=\lambda_{j}(x-\alpha_{j})$ and

$$ \displaystyle E_{j}(t,y_{j}) \displaystyle=\lambda_{j}^{4}\big(\Delta v_{j}-v_{j}-\delta_{j}|y_{j}|^{2}v_{j}\big) \displaystyle-\big(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{4}\delta_{j}\big)|y_{j}|^{2}v_{j}-\lambda_{j}\big(\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j}+(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2})\alpha_{j}\big)y_{j}v_{j} \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{2}\big(\dot{\gamma}_{j}+(\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j})\cdot\alpha_{j}+(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2})|\alpha_{j}|^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{2}\big)v_{j} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}\big(\dot{\lambda}_{j}+4\lambda_{j}\mu_{j}\big)\Lambda v_{j}-i\lambda_{j}^{3}\big(\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}-4\mu_{j}\alpha_{j}\big)\nabla v_{j} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Big(\frac{\partial v_{j}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\dot{\alpha}_{k}+\frac{\partial v_{j}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\dot{\beta}_{k}+\frac{\partial v_{j}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\dot{\lambda}_{k}+\frac{\partial v_{j}}{\partial\mu_{k}}\dot{\mu}_{k}+\frac{\partial v_{j}}{\partial\delta_{k}}\dot{\delta}_{k}\Big) \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{4}\bigg[\phi_{|v_{j}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\Big(\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)^{2}\phi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}\Big(\frac{\lambda_{k}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}+\lambda_{k}\alpha_{jk}\Big)\bigg]v_{j}. $$

Since we have

$$ \left(\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{j}}\right)^{2}\phi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}\Big(P(t),\frac{\lambda_{k}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}+\lambda_{k}\alpha_{jk}\Big)=-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}\frac{|v_{k}(P(t),\xi)|^{2}}{|\alpha_{jk}+\lambda_{j}^{-1}y_{j}-\lambda_{k}^{-1}\xi|^{2}}\mathrm{d}\xi, $$

we now consider the Taylor expansion

$$ \frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|^{2}}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)+O\left(\frac{|\zeta|^{N}}{|\alpha|^{N+2}}\right)\quad\text{as }\zeta\to 0, $$

where $F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)$ is homogeneous of degree $-n-1$ in $\alpha$ and of degree $n-1$ in $\zeta$ .

Similar to [12], [25] and as in [7, Section 3], let us define the approximation to be

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(N)}(t,y_{j}) \displaystyle:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\psi_{|v_{k}|^{2}}^{(n)}(t,y_{j}):=\sum_{n=1}^{N}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}|v_{k}(t,\xi)|^{2}F_{n}\big(\alpha_{jk},\lambda_{k}^{-1}\xi-\lambda_{j}^{-1}y_{j}\big)\mathrm{d}\xi, $$

and then make the ansatz

$$ v_{j}(t,y_{j}):=V_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),y_{j}):=Q(y_{j})+\delta_{j}\rho(y_{j})+W_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),y_{j}), $$

where the function $\rho(y_{j})$ is as in Lemma 2.1. We define

$$ R_{g}^{(N)}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_{j,g}^{(N)}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),x). $$

as the approximate solution. Omitting the subscript $g$ of $R^{(N)}$ for convenience, we write

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}R^{(N)}+\Delta R^{(N)}-\phi_{|R^{(N)}|^{2}}R^{(N)} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j})e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x+i\mu_{j}|x|^{2}}-\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(R_{k}^{(N)}\overline{R_{j}^{(N)}})}R^{(N)} \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\bigg[\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}-\Big(\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)^{2}\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}\Big(\frac{\lambda_{k}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}+\lambda_{k}\alpha_{jk}\Big)\bigg]V_{j}^{(N)}e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x+i\mu_{j}|x|^{2}}, $$

where now $E_{j}^{(N)}=\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}+S_{j}^{(N)}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{4}\Big(\Delta V_{j}^{(N)}-V_{j}^{(N)}-\phi_{\left|V_{j}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}V_{j}^{(N)}-\delta_{j}|y_{j}|^{2}V_{j}^{(N)}\Big)-\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\phi_{\left|V_{k}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N)}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}D_{j}^{(N)}\rho-\lambda_{j}B_{j}^{(N)}\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}+i\lambda_{j}M_{j}^{(N)}\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\bigg(\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot\big(2\beta_{k}+4\mu_{k}\alpha_{k}\big)+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\cdot\big(B_{k}^{(N)}-4\mu_{k}\beta_{k}-\lambda_{k}^{4}\delta_{k}\alpha_{k}\big) \displaystyle+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\big(M_{k}^{(N)}-4\mu_{k}\lambda_{k}\big)+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\mu_{k}}\big(\lambda_{k}^{4}\delta_{k}-4\mu_{k}^{2}\big)+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\delta_{k}}D_{k}^{(N)}\bigg) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle S_{j}^{(N)}(t,x) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-i\lambda_{j}^{3}\big(\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}-4\mu_{j}\alpha_{j}\big)\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}+i\lambda_{j}\big(\dot{\lambda}_{j}+4\lambda_{j}\mu_{j}-M_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\big(\dot{\delta}_{j}-D_{j}^{(N)}\big)\rho \displaystyle-\big(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{4}\delta_{j}\big)|y_{j}|^{2}V_{j}^{(N)}-\lambda_{j}\big(\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j}+(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2})\alpha_{j}-B_{j}^{(N)}\big)\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{2}\big(\dot{\gamma}_{j}+(\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j})\cdot\alpha_{j}+(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2})|\alpha_{j}|^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{2}\big)V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Bigg[\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot\left(\dot{\alpha}_{k}-2\beta_{k}-4\mu_{k}\alpha_{k}\right)+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta_{k}}\cdot\left(\dot{\beta}_{k}+4\mu_{k}\beta_{k}+\lambda_{k}^{4}\delta_{k}\alpha_{k}-B_{k}^{(N)}\right) \displaystyle+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\big(\dot{\lambda}_{k}+4\mu_{k}\lambda_{k}-M_{k}^{(N)}\big)+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\mu_{k}}\big(\dot{\mu}_{k}+4\mu_{k}^{2}-\lambda_{k}^{4}\delta_{k}\big)+\frac{\partial W_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\delta_{k}}\big(\dot{\delta}_{k}-D_{k}^{(N)}\big)\Bigg]. $$

Here the terms $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ are controlled by the nonlinear interactions and $S_{j}^{(N)}$ contains the modulation error. In particular, the approximation will be defined by comparing degrees of (parameter) homogeneity in $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ , where $M_{j}^{(N)}$ are free to choose and $B_{j}^{(N)},D_{j}^{(N)}$ are determined by orthogonality. The following notion of admissible functions will be useful.

#### Definition 3.1 (Admissible functions).

Recalling (3.1), let $\Omega$ denote the space of non-collision positions:

$$ \displaystyle\Omega:=\Big\{P=(\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu,\delta)\in\mathbb{R}^{4m}\times\mathbb{R}^{4m}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\ \big|\ \alpha_{j}\neq\alpha_{k},\ \forall j\neq k\Big\}. $$

(1) Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . Define $S_{n}$ to be the set of functions $\sigma:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ that is a finite sum of

$$ c\prod_{j\neq k}|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|^{-q_{jk}}(\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k})^{p_{jk}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}(\mu_{j}\alpha_{j})^{s_{j}}(\delta_{j}\alpha_{j})^{t_{j}}\beta_{j}^{k_{j}}\lambda_{j}^{l_{j}}\mu_{j}^{m_{j}}\delta_{j}^{n_{j}}, $$

where $c\in\mathbb{R}$ , $q_{jk}\in\mathbb{N}$ , $p_{jk}\in\N^{4}$ , $|p_{jk}|\leq q_{jk}$ , $s_{j},t_{j},k_{j}\in\mathbb{N}^{4}$ , $l_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}$ , $m_{j},n_{j}\in\mathbb{N}$ , and

$$ \begin{gathered}\sum_{j\neq k}(q_{jk}-|p_{jk}|)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\big(5m_{j}+7n_{j}+3|s_{j}|+5|t_{j}|\big)=n.\end{gathered} $$

(2) We say a function $u:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{4}\to\mathbb{C}$ is admissible if $u$ is a finite sum of

$$ z\sigma(\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\mu,\delta)\tau(x), $$

where $z\in\mathbb{C}$ , $\sigma\in S_{n}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\tau\in C^{\infty}$ satisfies

$$ \big|\nabla^{k}\tau(x)\big|\leq e^{-c_{k}|x|},\qquad\forall k\geq 0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{4}. $$

If $n$ is the same for all addends, then we say $u$ is admissible of degree $n$ . Otherwise, taking $n$ as the minimal one among all addends, we say $u$ is admissible of degree $\geq n$ .

#### Remark 3.2.

We stress that the above Definition 3.1 part (1) is different compared to [7, Section 3], and is crucial for us to extend the results there to hyperbolic-parabolic trajectories. The condition here is stronger. This is to compensate for the fact that $\alpha_{j}$ may grow faster than $\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}$ in the hyperbolic-parabolic case, as $|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|\sim t^{1/2}$ when $j,k$ are in the same cluster, while $|\alpha_{j}|\sim t$ . In other words, if we use the definition in [7, Section 3], then admissible functions may not decay in time.

The following lemma states the required decay of admissible functions.

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , $u$ be admissible of degree $\geq n$ and $P$ satisfy

$$ |\alpha|\lesssim a^{2},\ |\beta|\lesssim 1,\ \lambda\sim 1,\ |\mu|\lesssim a^{-5},\ |\delta|\lesssim a^{-7}, $$

then there are constants $c_{k}>0$ with

$$ |\nabla^{k}u(P,x)|\lesssim a^{-n}e^{-c_{k}|x|},\;\;k\geq 0,\;x\in\R^{4}. $$

The following proposition gives the construction of approximate solutions.

#### Proposition 3.4.

Given $m_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n+1}$ . For $n\geq 1$ and $1\leq j\leq m$ , there exist $d_{j}^{(n)},b_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n+1}$ and $T_{j}^{(n)}$ that is admissible of degree $n+1$ such that: for any $N\geq 1$ , if we set

$$ \displaystyle M_{j}^{(N)}(P)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}m_{j}^{(n)}(P),\;\;W_{j}^{(N)}(P,y_{j})=\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{j}^{(n)}(P,y_{j}), \displaystyle D_{j}^{(N)}(P)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_{j}^{(n)}(P),\quad B_{j}^{(N)}(P)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}b_{j}^{(n)}(P), $$

then $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ defined by (3.11) is admissible of degree $\geq N+2$ .

#### Proof.

The proof follows the identical procedure as in [7, Proposition 3.5] with the modified Definition 3.1 for admissible functions.

Let us proceed by induction over $N$ . Writing $T_{j}^{(n)}=X_{j}^{(n)}+iY_{j}^{(n)}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N+1)}-\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}= \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{4}\big(L_{+}X_{j}^{(N+1)}+iL_{-}Y_{j}^{(N+1)}\big)-\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q \displaystyle+i\lambda_{j}^{2}d_{j}^{(N+1)}\rho-\lambda_{j}b_{j}^{(N+1)}y_{j}Q+i\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+error, $$

where $error$ is (by induction) admissible of degree $\geq N+3$ . For this, the key observation is that the terms in (3.11) do not depend solely on $\alpha_{j}$ but rather on the terms

$$ \frac{(\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k})^{p_{jk}}}{|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|^{q_{jk}}}\;(k\neq j,\;|p_{jk}|\leq q_{jk}),\;\;\mu_{j}\alpha_{j},\;\;\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}.\;\; $$

which justifies the expression (3.14) given in Definition 3.1. Thus, in order to continue, it suffices to solve

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &L_{+}X_{j}^{(N+1)}=-\lambda_{j}^{-3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\\
&L_{-}Y_{j}^{(N+1)}=\lambda_{j}^{-2}d_{j}^{(N+1)}\rho+\lambda_{j}^{-3}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\end{aligned}\right. $$

where $\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ are the terms in $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ of degree $N+2$ . The existence of $X_{j}^{(N+1)}$ and $Y_{j}^{(N+1)}$ hence follows from Proposition 2.3 if

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\Big(-\lambda_{j}^{-3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\nabla Q\Big)=0,\\
&\Big(\lambda_{j}^{-2}d_{j}^{(N+1)}\rho+\lambda_{j}^{-3}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},Q\Big)=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Such $b_{j}^{(N+1)}$ and $d_{j}^{(N+1)}$ now always exist because $(y_{j}Q,\nabla Q)$ is invertible and $(\rho,Q)\neq 0$ . ∎

We conclude the section by a suitable estimate for the interaction error, which verifies the accuracy of approximate solutions we constructed above.

#### Proposition 3.5.

Let $V_{j}^{(N)}$ be as in Proposition 3.4. For $R_{g}^{(N)}$ defined by (3.9), let

$$ \Psi^{(N)}=i\partial_{t}R_{g}^{(N)}+\Delta R_{g}^{(N)}-\phi_{|R_{g}^{(N)}|^{2}}R_{g}^{(N)}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}S_{j}^{(N)}e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x+i\mu|x|^{2}}. $$

If we assume (3.18), then there exist constants $c,C>0$ such that

$$ |\Psi^{(N)}(t,x)|\leq\frac{C}{a^{N+2}(t)}\max\limits_{j=1,\dots,m}e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}(t)|},\;\;x\in\R^{4}. $$

The proof is as given in [7] and we refer to [7, Section 3] for details.

## 4. Trajectories

We now want to solve the following modulation equations, which by definition is the condition under which $S_{j}^{(N)}=0$ is obtained.

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}-4\mu_{j}\alpha_{j}=0,\\
&\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{4}\delta_{j}\alpha_{j}-B_{j}^{(N)}=0,\\
&\dot{\lambda}_{j}+4\lambda_{j}\mu_{j}-M_{j}^{(N)}=0,\\
&\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{4}\delta_{j}=0,\\
&\dot{\delta}_{j}-D_{j}^{(N)}=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Let us start by setting $m_{j}^{(n)}=0$ for $n\neq 2$ and

$$ m_{j}^{(2)}=-\frac{2\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\lambda_{j}}\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\alpha_{jk}\cdot\beta_{jk}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{4}}. $$

We will show we can take

$$ b_{j}^{(1)}=b_{j}^{(3)}=b_{j}^{(4)}=0,\quad b_{j}^{(2)}=-\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{4}} $$

and

$$ d_{j}^{(1)}=d_{j}^{(2)}=d_{j}^{(3)}=d_{j}^{(4)}=d_{j}^{(5)}=d_{j}^{(6)}=0. $$

We will also give an explicit expression of $d_{j}^{(7)}$ . For convenience, we let

$$ f=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}=-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{2\lambda_{j}^{2}}\Big(\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{1}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{2}}\Big),\quad h=-\lambda_{j}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}=m_{j}^{(2)}. $$

Note that $f$ only depends on $\alpha$ and $\lambda_{j}$ . Recall from the proof of Proposition 3.4 (c.f. [7, Proposition 3.5]) that we have

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &L_{+}\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(N+1)}=-\lambda_{j}^{-3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\\
&L_{-}\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(N+1)}=\lambda_{j}^{-2}d_{j}^{(N+1)}\rho+\lambda_{j}^{-3}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\end{aligned}\right. $$

and

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\Big(-\lambda_{j}^{-3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q-\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(N+1)}Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\nabla Q\Big)=0,\\
&\Big(\lambda_{j}^{-2}d_{j}^{(N+1)}\rho+\lambda_{j}^{-3}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+\lambda_{j}^{-4}\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},Q\Big)=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Since $\hat{E}_{j}^{(0)}=0$ and $\big(\sum\limits_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}Q,\nabla Q\big)=0$ , we take

$$ b_{j}^{(1)}=d_{j}^{(1)}=0,\quad T_{j}^{(1)}=f\Lambda Q. $$

Then we have

$$ \hat{E}_{j}^{(1)}=i\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(1)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}=-i\lambda_{j}h\Lambda Q. $$

Since $\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(1)}=0$ , $\mathrm{Im}\big(E_{j}^{(1)},Q\big)=0$ and by the choice of $m_{j}^{(2)}$ , we may take

$$ b_{j}^{(2)}=-\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{\alpha_{jk}}{|\alpha_{jk}|^{4}},\quad d_{j}^{(2)}=0,\quad T_{j}^{(2)}=0. $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\hat{E}_{j}^{(2)} \displaystyle=-\lambda_{j}^{4}\big(2\phi_{QT_{j}^{(1)}}T_{j}^{(1)}+\phi_{|T_{j}^{(1)}|^{2}}Q\big)-\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\Big(\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}T_{j}^{(1)}+2\psi_{QT_{k}^{(1)}}^{(1)}Q\Big) \displaystyle=-\lambda_{j}^{4}\big(2\phi_{QT_{j}^{(1)}}T_{j}^{(1)}+\phi_{|T_{j}^{(1)}|^{2}}Q\big)-\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}T_{j}^{(1)} \displaystyle=-\lambda_{j}^{4}f^{2}\Big(2\phi_{Q\Lambda Q}\Lambda Q+\phi_{(\Lambda Q)^{2}}Q+2\Lambda Q\Big). $$

By parity, we take

$$ b_{j}^{(3)}=d_{j}^{(3)}=0,\quad T_{j}^{(3)}=T_{j}^{(3)}(\alpha,\lambda)\text{ real valued}. $$

Moreover, since

$$ -\frac{1}{2}L_{+}(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)=2\phi_{Q\Lambda Q}\Lambda Q+\phi_{(\Lambda Q)^{2}}Q+2\Lambda Q, $$

we have

$$ T_{j}^{(3)}=\frac{f^{2}}{2}(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)-L_{+}^{-1}\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(3)}Q. $$

For two functions $u$ and $v$ , we write $u\equiv v$ if $u-v$ is an even function with exponential decay, and is $L^{2}$ -orthogonal to all radial functions with exponential decay. By the proof of Proposition 3.4, if we only want to determine the value of $b_{j}^{(n)}$ and $d_{j}^{(n)}$ , then we can do calculations up to $\equiv$ .

By [7, Lemma 4.2], we have $\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(3)}Q\equiv 0$ , and thus $L_{+}^{-1}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(3)}Q\equiv 0$ . This means

$$ T_{j}^{(3)}\equiv\frac{f^{2}}{2}(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q). $$

Then we have

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(3)}=-\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\Big(\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(2)}T_{j}^{(1)}+2\psi_{QT_{k}^{(1)}}^{(2)}Q\Big)-\lambda_{j}b_{j}^{(2)}y_{j}T_{j}^{(1)}=0 $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(3)} \displaystyle=\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(2)}\Lambda T_{j}^{(1)}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\bigg(\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(3)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(1)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}m_{k}^{(2)}\bigg) \displaystyle=\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(2)}\Lambda T_{j}^{(1)}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(1)}}{\partial\lambda_{j}}m_{j}^{(2)}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(3)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k} \displaystyle\equiv\lambda_{j}fh\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\lambda_{j}fh\Lambda Q-\lambda_{j}fh(\Lambda\Lambda Q-\Lambda Q)=0. $$

Since $\nabla\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(4)}\equiv 0$ in view of [7, Lemma 4.2], we take

$$ \begin{gathered}b_{j}^{(4)}=d_{j}^{(4)}=0,\quad T_{j}^{(4)}\equiv-L_{+}^{-1}\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(4)}Q.\end{gathered} $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(4)} \displaystyle=\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\bigg(\frac{\partial\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(1)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 4\mu_{k}\alpha_{k}\bigg) \displaystyle=\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 4\mu_{k}\alpha_{k}\Big)\Lambda Q $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(4)} \displaystyle=-\lambda_{j}^{4}\Big(2\phi_{QT_{j}^{(3)}}T_{j}^{(1)}+2\phi_{T_{j}^{(1)}T_{j}^{(3)}}Q+2\phi_{QT_{j}^{(1)}}T_{j}^{(3)}+\phi_{|T_{j}^{(1)}|^{2}}T_{j}^{(1)}\Big) \displaystyle\quad\ -\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\Big(\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(3)}T_{j}^{(1)}+2\psi_{QT_{k}^{(1)}}^{(3)}Q+\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}T_{j}^{(3)} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+2\psi_{QT_{k}^{(3)}}^{(1)}Q+\psi_{|T_{k}^{(1)}|^{2}}^{(1)}Q+2\psi_{QT_{k}^{(1)}}^{(1)}T_{j}^{(1)}\Big) \displaystyle\equiv-\lambda_{j}^{4}f^{3}\Big(\phi_{Q(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)}\Lambda Q+\phi_{\Lambda Q(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)}Q \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\ \ +\phi_{Q\Lambda Q}(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)+\phi_{(\Lambda Q)^{2}}\Lambda Q+(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)\Big). $$

Using parity and $(\Lambda Q,Q)=0$ , we have $(\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(4)},\nabla Q)=(\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(4)},Q)=0$ . Thus, we take

$$ b_{j}^{(5)}=d_{j}^{(5)}=0. $$

Moreover, since $\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(5)}Q\equiv 0$ by [7, Lemma 4.2] and

$$ \displaystyle-L_{+}(\Lambda\Lambda\Lambda Q-6\Lambda\Lambda Q+8\Lambda Q) \displaystyle=\phi_{Q(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)}\Lambda Q+\phi_{\Lambda Q(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)}Q \displaystyle\quad+\phi_{Q\Lambda Q}(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)+\phi_{(\Lambda Q)^{2}}\Lambda Q+(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q), $$

we have

$$ \displaystyle T_{j}^{(5)}\equiv \displaystyle\ \frac{f^{3}}{6}(\Lambda\Lambda\Lambda Q-6\Lambda\Lambda Q+8\Lambda Q)-i\lambda_{j}^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot\mu_{k}\alpha_{k}\Big)|y_{j}|^{2}Q \displaystyle\ +i\lambda_{j}^{-2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\partial L_{-}^{-1}\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}. $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(5)} \displaystyle=-2\lambda_{j}^{4}\phi_{QT_{j}^{(1)}}\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(4)}-\lambda_{j}^{4}\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{Q^{2},k}^{(1)}\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(4)}+\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(2)}\Lambda T_{j}^{(3)} \displaystyle\quad\ +\lambda_{j}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\bigg(\frac{\partial\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(5)}}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\cdot 2\beta_{k}-\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(1)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}4\mu_{k}\lambda_{k}+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(3)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}m_{k}^{(2)}\bigg) \displaystyle\equiv\lambda_{j}h\frac{f^{2}}{2}\Lambda(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q)-\lambda_{j}\frac{f^{2}}{2}h(\Lambda\Lambda\Lambda Q-6\Lambda\Lambda Q+8\Lambda Q) \displaystyle\quad\ +8\lambda_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}f\Lambda Q-2\lambda_{j}f^{2}h(\Lambda\Lambda Q-2\Lambda Q) \displaystyle=8\lambda_{j}^{2}\mu_{j}f\Lambda Q $$

and

#### Proposition 4.1.

Let $(\alpha^{\infty},\beta^{\infty})$ be a hyperbolic-parabolic solution of (1.10). Assume $\lambda^{\infty}\in\R_{+}^{m}$ and $\mu^{\infty}=\delta^{\infty}=0$ . Then there exists a solution $P^{(N)}$ of (4.1) such that

$$ \Big|P^{(N)}(t)-P^{\infty}(t)\Big|\to 0\text{ as }t\to+\infty. $$

For $(\alpha,\beta,\lambda)$ in $P^{(N)}$ we associate the cluster partition given by $(\alpha^{\infty},\beta^{\infty})$ .

#### Proof.

Take $\epsilon>0$ small. Define $Y=\Big\{P\in C\big([T_{0},+\infty),\Omega\big)\ \big|\ {\|P-P^{\infty}\|}_{1}\leq 1\Big\}$ , where

$$ {\|P\|}_{1}:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sup_{t\geq T_{0}}\Big(t^{\frac{1}{2}-3\epsilon}|\alpha_{j}(t)|+t^{\frac{3}{2}-3\epsilon}|\beta_{j}(t)|+t^{\frac{3}{2}-3\epsilon}|\lambda_{j}(t)|+t^{\frac{5}{2}-2\epsilon}|\mu_{j}(t)|+t^{\frac{7}{2}-\epsilon}|\delta_{j}(t)|\Big). $$

Note that if $\alpha_{j}^{\infty}$ and $\alpha_{k}^{\infty}$ are in the same cluster, then $\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}\sim t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $\beta_{jk}^{\infty}\sim t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ . If they are in different clusters, then $\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}\sim t$ and $\beta_{jk}^{\infty}\sim 1$ . We have respectively

$$ \frac{\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}\cdot\beta_{jk}^{\infty}}{|\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}|^{4}}\sim t^{-2}\;\;\text{(same cluster)},\;\;\;\frac{\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}\cdot\beta_{jk}^{\infty}}{|\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}|^{4}}\sim t^{-3}\;\;\text{(different clusters)}. $$

Thus $|d_{j}^{(7)}(P^{\infty})|\lesssim t^{-\frac{9}{2}}$ and particularly for $P\in Y$ we deduce $|d_{j}^{(7)}(P)|\leq t^{-\frac{9}{2}}$ . By the Taylor formula, we have

$$ b_{j}^{(2)}(P)-b_{j}^{(2)}(P^{\infty})=-\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\sum_{k\neq j}\left(\frac{\alpha_{jk}-\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}}{|\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}|^{4}}-\frac{4\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}\cdot(\alpha_{jk}-\alpha_{jk}^{\infty})}{|\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}|^{6}}\alpha_{jk}^{\infty}\right)+O(t^{-\frac{7}{2}+6\epsilon}). $$

Hence there exists $A_{j}\in\R^{4\times 4m}$ such that

$$ b_{j}^{(2)}(P)-b_{j}^{(2)}(P^{\infty})=\frac{A_{j}(\alpha-\alpha^{\infty})}{t^{2}}+O(t^{-3+3\epsilon}), $$

where $\alpha$ is understood as a column vector. Now let us set $A=(A_{1}^{T},\cdots,A_{m}^{T})^{T}\in\R^{4m\times 4m}$ , then (4.1) can be rewritten into

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\dot{\alpha}-\dot{\alpha}^{\infty}=2(\beta-\beta^{\infty})+O(t^{-\frac{3}{2}+2\epsilon}),\\
&\dot{\beta}-\dot{\beta}^{\infty}=\frac{A(\alpha-\alpha^{\infty})}{t^{2}}+O(t^{-\frac{5}{2}+2\epsilon}),\\
&\dot{\lambda}=O(t^{-\frac{3}{2}+2\epsilon}),\ \dot{\mu}=O(t^{-\frac{7}{2}+\epsilon}),\ \dot{\delta}=O(t^{-\frac{9}{2}}).\end{aligned}\right. $$

We then use the same argument as in [7] for (4.59) to conclude the claim. ∎

We have the following more precise estimate:

$$ |\alpha^{(N)}(t)-\alpha^{\infty}(t)|=o(t^{-\frac{1}{2}+}),\;|\beta^{(N)}(t)-\beta^{\infty}(t)|=o(t^{-\frac{3}{2}+}),\;|\lambda^{(N)}(t)-\lambda^{\infty}|=o(t^{-\frac{1}{2}+}), $$

and

$$ |\alpha^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim t,\;|\beta^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim 1,\;\lambda^{(N)}(t)\sim 1,\;|\mu^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{5}{2}},\;|\delta^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{7}{2}}. $$

Further, taking differences in (4.59), we have for any cluster $K$ and all $j,k\in K$

$$ |\alpha_{j}^{(N)}(t)-\alpha_{k}^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim t^{\frac{1}{2}},\;|\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t)-\beta_{k}^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{1}{2}},\;|\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)-\lambda_{k}^{(N)}(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where for the latter we make the assumption $\lambda_{j}^{\infty}=\lambda_{k}^{\infty}$ for all $K$ and $j,k\in K$ . We note the implicit constants only depend on $P^{\infty}$ .

## 5. Bootstrap reduction

We follow the strategy in [7, Section 5] (see also [25], [12]) and reduce the proof of Theorem 1.2 to a uniform backwards estimate.

#### Proposition 5.1 (Uniform bound).

Let $P^{(N)}$ be the solution of (4.1) in Proposition 4.1 and $\gamma_{j}^{(N)}(t)$ be such that

$$ \gamma_{j}^{(N)}(0)=0,\ \dot{\gamma}_{j}^{(N)}=(\lambda_{j}^{(N)})^{2}-|\beta_{j}^{(N)}|^{2}-\big(\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}+4\mu_{j}^{(N)}\beta_{j}^{(N)}\big)\cdot\alpha_{j}^{(N)}-\big(\dot{\mu}_{j}^{(N)}+4(\mu_{j}^{(N)})^{2}\big)|\alpha_{j}^{(N)}|^{2}. $$

For large $N$ there exists $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ such that if $(T_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $[T_{0},+\infty)$ with $T_{n}\to+\infty$ , we have the following. Let $u_{n}$ be the solution to

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &i\partial_{t}u_{n}+\Delta u_{n}-\phi_{|u_{n}|^{2}}u_{n}=0,\\
&u_{n}(T_{n},\cdot)=R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(T_{n},\cdot),\end{aligned}\right. $$

with backwards maximal interval $(t_{n},T_{n}]$ and $T_{*}\in[T_{0},T_{n}]\cap(t_{n},T_{n}]$ . Then if

$$ \left\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t)\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq 2t^{-\frac{N}{9}},\qquad\forall n\geq 1,\ \forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}], $$

also

$$ \left\|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t)\right\|_{H^{1}}\leq t^{-\frac{N}{9}},\qquad\forall n\geq 1,\ \forall t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

This proposition readily implies Theorem 1.2 as seen in [7] and similarly in [25]. For the proof of Theorem 1.2 by Proposition 5.1 we refer to [7, Section 5]. In order to prove Proposition 5.1, we deal with the zero modes of the linearized operators. The following lemma establishes a suitable modulation path $P$ with orthogonality conditions using the bootstrap assumption (5.3).

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $N,n\geq 1$ . Then there exist $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)>0$ and a unique modulation path $P$ given by parameters $g\in C^{1}([T_{0},+\infty),\Omega\times(\R/2\pi\Z)^{m})$ such that: if

$$ \varepsilon(t,x)=u_{n}(t,x)-R_{g}^{(N)}(t,x), $$

then for $t\geq T_{0}$ and $1\leq j\leq m$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}Q\Big)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}(xQ)\Big)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(|x|^{2}Q\big)\Big) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(\Lambda Q\big)\Big)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(\nabla Q\big)\Big)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\rho\Big)=0. $$

In particular, we have

$$ g(T_{n})=g^{(N)}(T_{n}),\quad\varepsilon(T_{n})=0. $$

For a proof let us refer to a similar argument in [25, Lemma 3.1]. With $P$ as in the previous lemma we now reduce Proposition 5.1 to the modulation estimate in the following bootstrap argument.

#### Proposition 5.3 (Bootstrap argument).

For $N$ and $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ large enough, $\forall n\geq 1,\ T_{*}\in[T_{0},T_{n}]\cap(t_{n},T_{n}]$ , if

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}\leq t^{-\frac{N}{4}},\quad\|x\varepsilon(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq t^{-\frac{N}{4}+2},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\lambda_{j}(t)-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\beta_{j}(t)-\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq t^{-1-\frac{N}{8}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\gamma_{j}(t)-\gamma_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq t^{-\frac{N}{8}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\mu_{j}(t)-\mu_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq t^{-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{N}{8}},\;\;\;\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\delta_{j}(t)-\delta_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq t^{-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{N}{8}},\end{aligned}\right. $$

for any $t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]$ , then

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{N}{4}},\quad\|x\varepsilon(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{N}{4}+2},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\lambda_{j}(t)-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\beta_{j}(t)-\beta_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-1-\frac{N}{8}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\gamma_{j}(t)-\gamma_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|+\left|\alpha_{j}(t)-\alpha_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{N}{8}},\\
&\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\mu_{j}(t)-\mu_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{N}{8}},\;\;\;\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\delta_{j}(t)-\delta_{j}^{(N)}(t)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}t^{-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{N}{8}}\end{aligned}\right. $$

for any $t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]$ .

The proof of Proposition 5.1 now follows directly from Proposition 5.3, where we use that (5.8) is implied by a bootstrap argument and

$$ \|u_{n}(t)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}\|_{H^{1}}\leq\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}+\|R_{g}^{(N)}-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}\|_{H^{1}}. $$

Thus (5.9) applies to estimate the right side with $t\geq T_{*}\geq T_{0}(N)$ large enough.

## 6. Modulation and error estimate

It remains to provide a proof of Proposition 5.3 which is the purpose of this section.

### 6.1. Modulation

We consider the modulation path $P$ in Lemma 5.2 and Proposition 5.3. Let us start by the observation that from (4.61) and (4.62), the bootstrap assumption (5.8) in Proposition 5.3 implies for $T_{0}\gg 1$ on $[T_{0},T_{n}]$

$$ \displaystyle|\alpha(t)|\lesssim t,\;|\beta(t)|\lesssim 1,\;|\lambda(t)|\sim 1,\;|\mu(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{5}{2}},\;|\delta(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{7}{2}}, \displaystyle|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{k}|\lesssim t^{\frac{1}{2}},\;\;|\beta_{j}-\beta_{k}|\lesssim t^{-\frac{1}{2}},\;\;|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k}|\lesssim t^{-\frac{1}{2}}, $$

where the latter line is true for any cluster $K$ and all $j,k\in K$ . Step 1. Modulation estimate. We write $u=u_{n}$ and let the error for the modulation equations (4.1) (as in [7, Section 6.1]) be defined as

$$ \displaystyle Mod(t):= \displaystyle\big|\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}-4\mu_{j}\alpha_{j}\big|+\big|\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j}+(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2})\alpha_{j}-B_{j}^{(N)}\big| \displaystyle+\big|\dot{\lambda}_{j}+4\lambda_{j}\mu_{j}-M_{j}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{4}\delta_{j}\big|+\big|\dot{\delta}_{j}-D_{j}^{(N)}\big| \displaystyle+\big|\dot{\gamma}_{j}+(\dot{\beta}_{j}+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j})\cdot\alpha_{j}+(\dot{\mu}_{j}+4\mu_{j}^{2})|\alpha_{j}|^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\lambda_{j}^{2}\big|, $$

where now $M_{j}^{(N)}=M_{j}^{(N)}(P),\;B_{j}^{(N)}=B_{j}^{(N)}(P),\;D_{j}^{(N)}=D_{j}^{(N)}(P)$ . Hence evaluating (1.1) in $u=\varepsilon+R$ with $R=R_{g}^{(N)}$ as in (3.9), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}\varepsilon+\Delta\varepsilon-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\varepsilon-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R=\Psi+\cN(\varepsilon)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}S_{j}(y_{j})e^{i(\gamma_{j}+\beta_{j}\cdot x+\mu_{j}|x|^{2})}, \displaystyle\cN(\varepsilon)=2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\varepsilon+\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}R+\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}\varepsilon, $$

where $\Psi=\Psi^{(N)}$ as defined in (3.22) is the interaction error.

#### Proposition 6.1.

We have for all $t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]$

$$ Mod(t)\leq\frac{C\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+C_{N}\big(a^{-N-2}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\big).\;\;\; $$

#### Proof.

The proof is as in [7, Section 6.1], hence let us give a sketch and spare details. We note for $\cN(\varepsilon)$ in (6.4) we have $|\cN(\varepsilon)|\lesssim\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ and in order to conclude (6.6) we now rely on the orthogonality conditions in Lemma 5.2. First let $\theta_{j}=g_{j}\theta$ be the modulation of a smooth decaying function, more precisely we require

$$ \displaystyle\theta_{j}(y_{j})=\lambda_{j}^{2}\theta(\lambda_{j}(x-\alpha_{j}))e^{i(\gamma_{j}+\beta_{j}\cdot x+\mu_{j}|x|^{2})},\;\;|\nabla^{k}\theta(x)|\leq C_{k}e^{-c_{k}|x|},\;\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{4},\;k\geq 0. $$

Considering (6.4) and taking $T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large enough we check that, after some careful calculation

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\bigg(\mathrm{Im}\int\varepsilon\overline{\theta_{j}}\;\mathrm{d}x\bigg)= \displaystyle-\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon\lambda_{j}^{2}\overline{(L_{j}\theta)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x+i\mu_{j}|x|^{2}}}-2\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R}_{j})}\sum_{k\neq j}\overline{R_{k}}\;\mathrm{d}x \displaystyle+\lambda_{j}^{6}\mathrm{Re}\int S_{j}\overline{\theta}+O_{N}\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{3}}+Mod\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+\frac{1}{a^{N+2}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right) $$

from Section 4, Proposition 3.5 and the definition of $Mod(t)$ . Here we have set

$$ L_{j}\theta:=-\Delta\theta+\theta+2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta\overline{V_{j}})}V_{j}+\bigg(\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}+\sum_{k\neq j}\psi_{|V_{k}|^{2}}^{(1)}\bigg)\theta. $$

Now let us choose $\theta$ to be either one of the functions $iQ,\;ixQ,\;i|x|^{2}Q,\;\Lambda Q,\;\nabla Q,\;\rho$ , then

$$ \displaystyle L_{j}\theta=f+O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{3}}\right)\left(e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+\frac{C_{N}}{a}e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right), \displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}=O\left(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{3}}\right)\big(1+|x-\alpha_{j}|\big)^{2}, $$

$$ Mod(t)\leq\frac{C\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{2}}+\frac{C_{N}}{a^{N+2}}+C_{N}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\;\;t\in[T_{*},T_{n}], $$

Step 2. Integration of the modulation estimate. We are now concerned with the second, third and fourth line of (5.9) assuming (5.8) in Proposition 5.3. $$ \displaystyle|\dot{\alpha}_{j}-\dot{\alpha}_{j}^{(N)}|\leq Ct^{-1-\frac{N}{8}},\;\;|\dot{\mu}_{j}-\dot{\mu}_{j}^{(N)}|\leq Ct^{-\frac{7}{2}-\frac{N}{8}}. $$

which likewise implies the claim in (5.9) for $\alpha_{j},\mu_{j}$ taking $N\gg 1$ large. Finally, for the phase $\gamma_{j}$ we collect the above estimates and infer

$$ \displaystyle|\dot{\gamma}_{j}-\dot{\gamma}_{j}^{(N)}| \displaystyle\leq C\Big(|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{j}^{(N)}|+|\beta_{j}-\beta_{j}^{(N)}|+a|\dot{\beta}_{j}-\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}|+\frac{|\alpha_{j}-\alpha_{j}^{(N)}|}{a^{2}} \displaystyle\qquad\;\;+a|\mu_{j}\beta_{j}-\mu_{j}^{(N)}\beta_{j}^{(N)}|+a^{2}|\dot{\mu}_{j}-\dot{\mu}_{j}^{(N)}|\Big)+Mod(t)\leq Ct^{-1-\frac{N}{8}}. $$

### 6.2. Error estimate

Here we give a proof of the first line of the bootstrap estimate (5.9). The argument follows [7, Section 6.2], [12], [25] and we first observe the by expanding the energy via $u=R+\varepsilon$ we have the conservation law

$$ \displaystyle 2\mathcal{E}(u_{0})= \displaystyle\;\;2\mathcal{E}(R)-2\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon,\overline{\Delta R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}R})+\mathcal{G}_{1}(\varepsilon) $$

where the nonlinear part reads

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{1}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\;\int|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\kappa\int|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|^{2}+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-\frac{\kappa}{2}\int|\nabla\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}|^{2}. $$

For deriving (5.9) it is not enough to estimate the interactions $\mathcal{G}_{1}(\varepsilon)$ in (6.24) and thus we add localizations of mass, momentum, their center and the variance along $\alpha(t)$ to $\mathcal{G}_{1}(\varepsilon)$ . First let us note the following and refer to a similar proof in [25, Section 4.2].

#### Lemma 6.2.

There exist $c,C>0$ and $\varphi_{j}\in C^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{4})$ for $1\leq j\leq m$ such that

$$ \begin{gathered}0\leq\varphi_{j}(t,x)\leq 1,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{m}\varphi_{j}(t,x)\equiv 1,\;\;|\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|+|\nabla\varphi_{j}|\leq\frac{C}{a},\quad|\partial_{t}\sqrt{\varphi_{j}}|+|\nabla\sqrt{\varphi_{j}}|\leq\frac{C}{a},\\
\varphi_{j}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1,\quad|x-\alpha_{j}(t)|\leq ca(t),\\
&0,\quad|x-\alpha_{k}(t)|\leq ca(t),\ k\neq j.\end{aligned}\right.\end{gathered} $$

Moreover, for any cluster $K$ we have

$$ \begin{gathered}|\partial_{t}\varphi_{K}|+|\nabla\varphi_{K}|\leq Ct^{-1},\quad\text{where }\varphi_{K}=\sum_{j\in K}\varphi_{j}.\end{gathered} $$

The cut-off functions $\varphi_{j}$ localize the approximate solution $R$ in (3.9) of Section 3 to $R_{j}$ . To be precise, we have, using Lemma 3.3 for some $c>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{x\in\R^{4}}|\varphi_{j}(t)R(t)-R_{j}(t)|\leq C_{N}e^{-ca(t)},\;\;t\geq T_{0}. $$

We now define (see [7, Section 6.2]) the functional $\displaystyle\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{k=1}^{5}\mathcal{G}_{k}(\varepsilon),$ where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{2}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\;\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2},\;\;\;\mathcal{G}_{3}(\varepsilon)=\;-2\sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon}), \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{4}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\;4\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{j}^{2}\int\varphi_{j}|x|^{2}|\varepsilon|^{2},\;\;\;\mathcal{G}_{5}(\varepsilon)=\;4\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{j}\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}x|\varepsilon|^{2}-4\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(x\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon}). $$

and note the latter $\mathcal{G}_{4},\mathcal{G}_{5}$ are specific to the $L^{2}$ -critical case, i.e. to $d=4$ dimensions (c.f. [25]). Remaining steps. In order to conclude the first line of (5.9), we need coercivity for $\mathcal{G}$ in Proposition 6.3 which will be combined with an upper bound in Proposition 6.4 assuming the bootstrap condition (5.8).

#### Proposition 6.3.

Let $N\geq 2$ . For $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large enough, there exists $c_{0}>0$ such that

$$ \mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))\geq c_{0}\|\varepsilon(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\;\;t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]. $$

#### Sketch of proof.

The proof follows as provided below [7, Proposition 6.3] and relies on Lemma 2.2 part (2) in Section 2 combined with the orthogonality in (5.6) of Lemma 5.2. Let $\varepsilon_{j}=\varepsilon\sqrt{\varphi_{j}}$ and $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}=g_{j}^{-1}\varepsilon_{j}$ , that is we define

$$ \tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}(t,y_{j})=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}(t)}\varepsilon_{j}(t,\lambda_{j}^{-1}(t)y_{j}+\alpha_{j}(t))e^{-i(\gamma_{j}(t)+\beta_{j}(t)\cdot(\lambda_{j}^{-1}y_{j}+\alpha_{j}(t))+\mu_{j}|\lambda_{j}^{-1}y_{j}+\alpha_{j}(t)|^{2})}. $$

For $T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large enough we then have

$$ \Big(L_{+}\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}),\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})\Big)+\Big(L_{-}\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}),\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j})\Big)\geq c\|\tilde{\varepsilon}_{j}\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\quad\forall t\geq T_{0} $$

and define the truncated functionals

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j,\varphi}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\int\varphi_{j}|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R_{j}|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\kappa\int\big|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{{R_{j}}})}\big|^{2} \displaystyle+\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2}-4\mu_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(x\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon})-2\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon}) \displaystyle+4\mu_{j}\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}x|\varepsilon|^{2}+4\mu_{j}^{2}\int\varphi_{j}|x|^{2}|\varepsilon|^{2}. $$

Therefore we obtain, after some calculations (for details see the proof of [7, Proposition 6.3]), using (6.31), Lemma 3.3 and (6.26),(6.28)

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j,\varphi}(\varepsilon)\geq c\int\varphi_{j}(|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+|\varepsilon|^{2})-\frac{C_{N}}{a}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Further by Lemma 6.2 we can rewrite

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathcal{H}_{j,\varphi}(\varepsilon)+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-\frac{\kappa}{2}\int|\nabla\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}|^{2} \displaystyle+\sum_{j\neq k}\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(R_{k}\overline{R_{j}})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\kappa\sum_{j\neq k}\int\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{j}})}\cdot\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{k}})}. $$

The first term is thus estimated by (6.33), whereas the other terms in the first line are $O\big(t^{-N/4}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\big)$ by Proposition 3.5 and the bootstrap assumption (5.8). The two terms in the second line are $O_{N}\big(e^{-ca}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\big)$ and $O_{N}\Big(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{a}\Big)$ , respectively. This shows the claim after taking $T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large enough. ∎

#### Proposition 6.4.

Let us assume (5.8) in Proposition 5.3. For $N\geq 2$ and $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large enough, there exists $C,C_{N}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))|\leq\frac{C}{N}t^{-\frac{N}{2}}+C_{N}t^{-\frac{3N}{4}}. $$

for all $t\in[T_{*},T_{n}]$ .

#### Proof.

We omit some details for the following calculation found in the proof of [7, Proposition 6.4]. First using integration by parts we have for $T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large by (6.4) and Proposition 3.5

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\varepsilon) \displaystyle=O\big(Mod(t)\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\big)+O_{N}\left(\frac{1}{a^{N+2}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\right) \displaystyle+4\mathrm{Re}\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\varepsilon\partial_{t}\overline{R}+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\partial_{t}R\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}+2\mathrm{Re}\int\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}\varepsilon\partial_{t}\overline{R}, $$

where we note $|S_{j}(t,x)|\leq CMod(t)e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}$ . Further since (for $T_{0}(N)\gg 1$ large)

$$ \displaystyle|V_{j}^{(N)}(y_{j})|\leq Ce^{-c|y_{j}|}+C_{N}a^{-1}e^{-c_{N}|y_{j}|}, \displaystyle|R_{g,j}^{(N)}(x)|\leq Ce^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}+C_{N}a^{-1}e^{-c|x-\alpha_{j}|}, \displaystyle|M_{j}^{(N)}|+|B_{j}^{(N)}|+|D_{j}^{(N)}|\leq Ca^{-2}+C_{N}a^{-3}, $$

the estimate (6.1) implies the following for $R_{j}=g_{j}V_{j}$

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}R_{j}=-2\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla R_{j}+i\big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\big)R_{j}+\left(O_{N}\Big(\frac{1}{a^{3}}\Big)+O\Big(Mod+\frac{C}{t}\Big)\right)e^{-c_{N}|x-\alpha_{j}|}. $$

Hence applying (6.6) in Proposition 6.1, we infer

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Bigg(4\Big( \displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Im}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{j}})-8\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla\overline{R_{j}}) \displaystyle-4\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla R_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}|\varepsilon|^{2}\Bigg)+O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{t}\right)+O_{N}\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{N+2}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right), $$

where we used Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev’s estimate and a straight forward adaption of the distance estimates in [25, Lemma 2.3] for $d=4$ dimensions. Moreover by integration by parts, (6.1), (6.4) and the bound for $S_{j}$ as above, we likewise have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{2}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\varepsilon) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\big[4\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R\overline{\varepsilon})+\int\Big(\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2}+2\nabla\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon})\Big)\big] \displaystyle+O_{N}\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{N+1}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right)+O(Mod(t)\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}), $$

where we recall $|\Psi|\lesssim a^{-N-2},\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)\lesssim\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ implying the first term in the second line. Let us note by the modulation estimate (6.6) and the localization property of $\varphi_{j}$ in (6.28) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\big[\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R\overline{\varepsilon})+O(Mod(t)\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}) \displaystyle=\;-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Im}(\overline{R}_{j}\varepsilon)+O\big(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{N+2}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\big)+O_{N}\big(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{t}\big). $$

For the remaining terms in (6.42) we consider the clusters $K$ and select (arbitrary) $\lambda_{K},\beta_{K}$ such that $\lambda_{j}^{2}=\lambda_{K}^{2}+O(t^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ and $|\beta_{j}|^{2}=|\beta_{K}|^{2}+O(t^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ for all $j\in K$ by (6.2). Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\Big(\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2}+2\nabla\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon})\Big) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{l}\Big(\lambda_{K_{i}}^{2}+|\beta_{K_{i}}|^{2}\Big)\int\Big(\partial_{t}\varphi_{K_{i}}|\varepsilon|^{2}+2\nabla\varphi_{K_{i}}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon})\Big)+O_{N}\big(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{t}\big) \displaystyle=O_{N}\big(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{t}\big), $$

where we used $|\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|+|\nabla\varphi_{j}|=O(t^{-1/2})$ in the second line and (6.27) to conclude the third line. Similarly we compute (for more details see [7, Section 6.2])

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{3}}{\mathrm{d}t} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(8\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla\overline{R_{j}})+4\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla R_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}|\varepsilon|^{2}\right) \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\beta_{j}\int\bigg(\nabla\varphi_{j}\Big(2|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})+\phi_{|R|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}\Big)+\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon})\bigg) \displaystyle+O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{t}\right)+O_{N}\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}}{a^{N+2}}+\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{a^{2}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right). $$

Then the second line is of order $O\left(\frac{\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}}{t}\right)$ by the cluster decomposition for $\beta_{j}$ as in $\mathcal{G}_{2}$ above, i.e. we note by (6.2), (6.26) and (6.27) we have

$$ |\beta_{K}|\Big(|\partial_{t}\varphi_{K}|+|\nabla\varphi_{K}|\Big)+\max_{j\in K}\Big[|\beta_{j}-\beta_{K}|\cdot\Big(|\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|+|\nabla\varphi_{j}|\Big)\Big]\leq\frac{C}{t} $$

for any fixed representative $\beta_{K}$ of the $\beta_{j}$ ’s of a cluster $K$ . Combining the previous calculations, we hence deduce using the bootstrap assumption (5.8) and integration

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{G}_{1}(\varepsilon)+\mathcal{G}_{2}(\varepsilon)+\mathcal{G}_{3}(\varepsilon)|\leq \displaystyle\int_{t}^{T_{n}}C\tau^{-\frac{N}{2}-1}+C_{N}\tau^{-\frac{3N}{4}-1}\;\mathrm{d}\tau \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{C}{N}t^{-\frac{N}{2}}+C_{N}t^{-\frac{3N}{4}}. $$

For the estimates of $\mathcal{G}_{4}(\varepsilon),\mathcal{G}_{5}(\varepsilon)$ , we refer to (4) and (5) of the proof of [7, Proposition 6.4] and the fact $|\mu_{j}(t)|\lesssim t^{-\frac{5}{2}},|\beta_{j}(t)|\lesssim 1$ . Precisely, via applying again (3.12), (6.6), (6.4) and Proposition 3.5 to $\frac{d}{dt}\int|x\varepsilon|^{2}$ for estimating $|\mathcal{G}_{4}(\varepsilon)|$ and using Cauchy-Schwarz for $\mathcal{G}_{5}(\varepsilon)$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{G}_{4}(\varepsilon)|\leq\frac{C}{N}t^{-\frac{N}{2}}+C_{N}t^{-\frac{3N}{4}},\;\;|\mathcal{G}_{5}(\varepsilon)|\leq\frac{C}{N}t^{-\frac{N}{2}}. $$

This completes the proof. ∎

The final proof of the bootstrap Proposition 5.3 is now a combination of the above Propositions.

#### Proof of (5.9).

It remains to check the first line. Note that by (6.18) in [7, Section 6.2], which is the same upper bound of $|\mathcal{G}_{4}(\varepsilon)|$ in (6.49) but for $\|x\varepsilon\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ , we get the bound for $\|x\varepsilon\|_{L^{2}}$ in (5.9). Then combining (6.35) in Proposition 6.4 and the coercivity of $\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)$ in Proposition 6.3, we take $N$ and $T_{0}=T_{0}(N)$ subsequently large to conclude the claim. ∎
